title: Bridging AI and Emotion: Enhanced Models for Personal Finance Manager Applications
venue: International Journal of Computing and Digital Systems
tldr: Integrating sentiment analysis with Transformer, TCN, and N-BEATS models for spending prediction reduces MAPE from 10.5% to 7.8% and achieves 92% anomaly detection accuracy.
problem_and_motivation: Contemporary personal finance applications rely on fixed, rule-based structures that cannot analyze unstructured user data such as mood, preferences, and spending frequency. They process structured data effectively but fail to extract value from transaction descriptions and user behavioral signals, leading to irrelevant recommendations. There is a gap between conventional financial advisory platforms and advanced AI-driven solutions that can adapt to individual users.
approach: The system is built on .NET Core 6 for backend scalability and Python with TensorFlow and Keras for AI-driven analytical components.
Three AI modules are integrated: anomaly detection, sentiment analysis, and predictive modeling for financial insights.
Anomaly detection employs Isolation Forest, LOF, and One-Class SVM to identify fraudulent transactions and unusual spending patterns in real time.
Sentiment analysis uses fine-tuned BERT and GPT language models on transaction descriptions to classify user emotions into predefined types.
Predictive modeling compares Transformer, TCN, and N-BEATS architectures for forecasting future spending from historical transaction sequences.
The dataset aggregates bank transaction logs, Merchant Category Code classifications, merchant demographics, and account data for model training and evaluation.
K-fold cross-validation and stratified sampling are used to evaluate model performance, with hyperparameter tuning via grid search and random search.
A feedback loop integrates user confirmations and corrections to continuously refine anomaly detection, sentiment classification, and spending predictions.
findings: num: MAPE improved from 10.5% to 7.8% when sentiment analysis was incorporated into predictive models.
num: Anomaly detection achieved 92% accuracy, 90% precision, 85% recall, 87.5% F1-score, and 0.93 ROC-AUC score.
num: Predictive accuracy reached 88% alignment with actual user behavior within a 90% confidence interval.
num: N-BEATS achieved the lowest RMSE of 0.057, outperforming Transformer (0.062) and TCN (0.074).
num: Sentiment-integrated models reduced prediction error by 25% compared to rule-based budgeting systems.
num: Variations greater than 5% from typical spending patterns are flagged as anomalies for user review.
Sentiment analysis improves predictive model accuracy even when the underlying model architecture remains unchanged.
Real-time anomaly detection operates without constant human intervention, making it scalable for high-volume financial environments.
Collaborative filtering and MCC-based merchant matching deliver personalized offers and discounts based on user transaction history.
The TCN model with sentiment data does not always improve predictive performance, suggesting sentiment alignment varies by architecture.

Root Mean Squared Error quantifies prediction deviation across all test instances.

Root Mean Squared Error, a measure of the average magnitude of prediction errors.
Receiver Operating Characteristic Area Under Curve, a metric for binary classification performance.

A deep learning architecture using self-attention mechanisms for sequence modeling.
Temporal Convolutional Network, a sequence model using causal convolutions for time-series data.
Neural Basis Expansion Analysis for interpretable time-series forecasting, decomposing data into trend and seasonality.
An anomaly detection algorithm that isolates observations by random feature and split-value selection.
Local Outlier Factor, a density-based algorithm that detects anomalies by comparing local neighborhood densities.
A support vector machine variant that learns a decision boundary separating normal data from outliers.
Bidirectional Encoder Representations from Transformers, a pre-trained language model for text understanding.
Generative Pre-trained Transformer, a language model used for text classification and generation.
A cross-platform, high-performance framework for building backend web applications and services.

topic_relevance.contribution_to_field: This paper contributes an integrated AI-driven financial advisory framework that combines three distinct analytical capabilities: sentiment analysis, predictive spending modeling, and real-time anomaly detection. It provides empirical evidence that incorporating sentiment data from transaction descriptions improves deep learning model accuracy, reducing prediction error by 25% compared to rule-based approaches. The study benchmarks Transformer, TCN, and N-BEATS architectures on bank transaction data, establishing N-BEATS as the best performer for spending pattern forecasting. The work also demonstrates a multi-model anomaly detection approach using Isolation Forest, LOF, and One-Class SVM that achieves superior precision and recall over traditional fraud detection systems.
directly_justifies: Integrating sentiment analysis with predictive models reduces MAPE from 10.5% to 7.8% for spending forecasting.
Anomaly detection using Isolation Forest, LOF, and One-Class SVM achieves 92% accuracy and 0.93 ROC-AUC on financial transactions.
N-BEATS outperforms Transformer and TCN models on spending prediction with RMSE of 0.057.
Sentiment-integrated models achieve 88% alignment with actual user behavior within 90% confidence interval.
A multi-model anomaly detection approach adapts dynamically to evolving fraud patterns unlike static rule-based systems.
limits: The study does not report sample size, number of users, or duration of the data collection period.
Experimental results lack statistical significance testing, confidence intervals on reported metrics, and ablation studies.
The paper acknowledges limited generalization across diverse financial behaviors and demographics.
Scalability to large-scale real-world financial data streams is not empirically validated.
User trust and adoption factors are identified as limitations but not experimentally investigated.
topic_relevance.topic_mapping_rationale: All 14 topic domains were systematically scanned. Domain 1 (Filipino Young Professionals) and Domain 2 (Culturally Specific Financial Practices) were flagged as irrelevant because the study uses bank transaction data without demographic or cultural specificity to the Philippines. Domain 3 was partially relevant through MCC-based expense categorization (3.A medium) though category design considerations (3.B) are only contextually addressed. Domain 4 was flagged as medium relevance because the paper compares against Mint, YNAB, and traditional banking fraud systems, identifying gaps in existing platforms. Domain 5 received high relevance (5.A) for its core contribution of classifying users into emotional spending profiles via NLP sentiment analysis, though cold-start dynamics (5.B) and formal classification methodologies (5.C) received low and medium respectively. Domain 6 is a primary focus with high relevance for predictive modeling (6.A) and forecasting algorithms (6.B) across Transformer, TCN, and N-BEATS architectures. Domain 7 was flagged as medium for its budgeting features (7.A, 7.B) though constrained optimization (7.C) and infeasibility handling (7.D) are not addressed. Domain 8 is a core contribution with high relevance for both anomaly detection systems (8.A) and specific algorithms (8.B) including Isolation Forest, LOF, and One-Class SVM, though cold-start baselines (8.C) are not discussed. Domain 9 received low relevance as mobile UX is mentioned only as a front-end delivery channel. Domain 10 (data privacy and security) was flagged as medium for its security discussions, while user trust (10.B) is acknowledged as a limitation and consent management (10.C) is not addressed. Domain 11 was flagged as medium for engagement dynamics driven by merchant recommendations and feedback loops. Domain 12 received high relevance for algorithmic evaluation (12.B) with detailed metrics and cross-validation, and medium for the broader system evaluation (12.A). Domain 13 (savings and debt management) received low relevance as goal-setting features are described without methodological depth. Domain 14 received medium relevance for model serving and deployment (14.B) discussions, while synthetic data (14.A) and on-device inference (14.C) are not applicable. The paper primarily covers predictive modeling, anomaly detection, and sentiment analysis domains, with secondary coverage of budgeting, evaluation, and existing system landscapes.

limitations: The study does not disclose sample size, dataset volume, or user demographics, limiting reproducibility and generalization assessment.
No statistical significance testing or confidence intervals are provided for the reported performance metrics.
The paper acknowledges that generalization across diverse financial behaviors and demographics needs further investigation.
Computational efficiency and resource requirements of the deep learning models are not measured or discussed.
The paper acknowledges that user trust and adoption challenges remain as critical future research areas.
No ablation study is provided to isolate the individual contribution of sentiment analysis versus model architecture improvements.
The 5% threshold for flagging anomalies as suspicious is presented without sensitivity analysis or justification.
